entities.name: Methodist Church of Great Britain
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Methodist Church of Great Britain, formally constituted in 1784 when John Wesley (an Anglican priest who never formally left the Church of England) died and his movement became independent, is the world's founding Methodist body and the parent denomination of 80 million Methodists worldwide — the largest Protestant family after Lutheranism and Reformed traditions. Methodism's social mission — prioritizing the working poor, opposing slavery, establishing Sunday schools, and founding hospitals — made it the defining working-class religious movement of the Industrial Revolution.

John Wesley, an Oxford-educated Anglican priest, experienced his 'Aldersgate conversion' on May 24, 1738 — feeling his heart 'strangely warmed' — and became an open-air evangelist preaching to miners, factory workers, and the urban poor excluded from Anglican parish churches. Wesley rode 250,000 miles on horseback across Britain and Ireland, delivered 40,000 sermons, and organized converts into 'classes' — small accountability groups of 12 that became the template for cell church movements globally.

Methodism's practical Christianity pioneered: Sunday Schools (Robert Raikes, 1780, providing working-class children their only education), hospital founding (Wesley's Dispensary, 1746), prison reform advocacy (alongside Quakers), and the most vocal early anti-slavery movement (Wesley's last letter was to William Wilberforce encouraging abolition). American Methodism (founded from British parent) became America's largest denomination by 1850, with circuit riders carrying Wesley's message to frontier settlements. The YMCA, Salvation Army, and many other social welfare organizations trace their heritage to Methodist working-class ministry.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Methodism's Sunday Schools provided literacy to millions of Industrial Revolution working-class children — creating the educational foundation for the labor movement — while its anti-slavery advocacy contributed to abolition, making it the most socially consequential Protestant denomination in history.
